title: A Coffin in Egypt
summary: Jacob is embalmed, mourned, and buried at Machpelah; Joseph reassures his fearful brothers that God meant their evil for good, and dies trusting God’s promised visitation.
historicalContext: Jacob died seventeen years after coming down to Egypt (47:28), when Joseph was about fifty-six, and Joseph lived on for more than half a century. Egyptian funerary practice surrounds the opening scene: skilled embalmers who removed the organs and dried the body in natron over many weeks, public mourning that rivalled the honours paid to a king, and an official cortège of court dignitaries with chariots and horsemen. Egyptians placed their tombs in the west, the land of the setting sun, and furnished them for an afterlife among the gods; Jacob insisted on being carried east to a cave in Canaan bought by Abraham from Ephron the Hittite (23:16-20). The route of the funeral party appears to have curved around the Dead Sea to a site near the Jordan. Joseph’s age of 110 years matched the ideal span of life in Egyptian wisdom, and his embalmed body waited in Egypt until Moses carried it out at the exodus (Exodus 13:19).
literaryContext: Genesis 50 completes the scene that began at 47:28 with Jacob’s request to be buried in Canaan, and it closes both the Joseph story and the book. Three movements follow one another. The burial of Jacob (vv. 1-14) is told with the vocabulary of the coming exodus: going up, little ones and flocks left behind, Egyptian chariots and horsemen, a crossing toward the land of promise. The brothers’ fear (vv. 15-21) returns to the wound of chapter 37 and draws from Joseph the book’s clearest statement of providence, echoing 45:5-8. Joseph’s last days (vv. 22-26) mirror his father’s: a deathbed charge, an oath, a promise that God will visit and bring the family up. The book that opened with life breathed into dust in a garden ends with a dead man in a coffin in Egypt, yet the final word in Joseph’s mouth is hope, and the story runs straight on into Exodus 1.
themes: Burial as a confession of faith in the promised land
Forgiveness that refuses to take God’s place
Providence overruling human evil for good
Death as sleep awaiting God’s visitation
The promise carried from one generation to the next

outline.title: Mourning and Embalming in Egypt
outline.summary: Joseph weeps over his father, has him embalmed, and after seventy days of national mourning obtains Pharaoh’s leave to bury him in Canaan as he had sworn.

outline.title: The Funeral Journey to Machpelah
outline.summary: A great company of Egyptians and Israelites goes up to the threshingfloor of Atad for seven days of lamentation, and Jacob’s sons bury him in Abraham’s cave before returning to Egypt.

outline.title: Fear Answered by Forgiveness
outline.summary: Afraid that Joseph will now take revenge, the brothers plead for forgiveness and offer themselves as slaves; Joseph declines God’s place, declares that God meant their evil for good, and promises to provide for them.

outline.title: Joseph’s Last Charge and Death
outline.summary: Joseph lives to see his great-grandchildren, assures his kin that God will surely visit them and bring them to the promised land, binds them by oath to carry up his bones, and dies in Egypt.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph fell upon his father's face, and wept upon him, and kissed him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter division falls awkwardly, for the verse continues straight from 49:33, where Jacob gathered up his feet into the bed and breathed his last. Before anything is said about funerals, courtiers, or Pharaoh, the narrator shows a son bent over his father’s body. Joseph “fell upon his father’s face, and wept upon him, and kissed him.” The three verbs are simple and physical. God had told Jacob at Beersheba that Joseph would “put his hand upon thine eyes” (46:4), and the promise is kept in this scene: the son Jacob had mourned as torn by beasts is the one who closes his eyes.

Only Joseph’s grief is described, which need not mean the other sons felt nothing. Joseph is the most openly emotional figure in Genesis; he has wept on meeting his brothers, on seeing Benjamin, on revealing himself, and on embracing his father in Goshen (42:24; 43:30; 45:2, 14; 46:29). Here his tears are those of bereavement. The kiss is the gesture of farewell, the same that Laban gave his daughters and grandchildren when he parted from them (31:55).

Scripture never treats grief at death as a failure of faith. Abraham came “to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her” (23:2), and Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus while knowing he would raise him (John 11:35). Paul does not forbid believers to sorrow; he asks them not to sorrow “as others which have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Joseph’s tears and his later insistence on burial in Canaan belong together: he grieves a real loss and still holds to the promise his father died believing.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּבְךְּ עָלָיו וַיִּשַּׁק־לוֹ (vayyevk ‘alayw vayyishshaq-lo) — and wept upon him, and kissed him
wordNotes.explanation: Bakah is the ordinary verb for weeping aloud, and it marks the turning points of Joseph’s story. The preposition “upon” pictures him bent over the body. Nashaq, “to kiss,” is used for greeting and for farewell; Joseph had kissed his brothers when he made himself known (45:15), and Orpah kissed Naomi when she parted from her (Ruth 1:14). Here it is the last kiss given to the dead.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father: and the physicians embalmed Israel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph turns from grief to action, giving orders as a man of rank: “Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father.” Embalming was an Egyptian art. The internal organs were removed and stored in jars, the body cavity was cleansed and packed with spices, and the corpse was dried in natron before being wrapped in linen and coated with resin. It was costly and lengthy, reserved for those of means, and here it is given to a Hebrew herdsman because his son governs Egypt.

The text names physicians, not priests. In Egypt the treatment of the dead was bound up with religion, since the body was preserved so that the dead person could live on in the world beyond and enjoy the offerings left in the tomb. Genesis mentions none of that apparatus: no spells, no grave goods, no offerings to the gods of the west. What is recorded is a physical procedure carried out by medical men. The purpose that the narrative supplies is practical. Jacob had bound Joseph by oath to bury him in Canaan (47:29-31), and a body could not otherwise survive the weeks of preparation and the long journey north.

The verse ends by calling the dead man “Israel,” the covenant name given at Peniel (32:28). It is a reminder of whose body this is. Israel’s faith did not place the hope of the dead in preserving flesh. The dead return to dust (3:19) and “know not any thing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5); they sleep until God calls them, and their hope is resurrection, the promise Daniel would one day hear stated plainly (Daniel 12:2). Joseph could accept an Egyptian technique without accepting the beliefs behind it, because the body was being prepared for a grave in the land of promise.

wordNotes.term: הָרֹפְאִים (harofe’im) — the physicians
wordNotes.explanation: The participle of rapha’, “to heal,” describes those who practise healing. Scripture otherwise uses it of doctors consulted for illness, as when Asa “sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” (2 Chronicles 16:12). Its use here for embalmers suggests that Joseph employed medical practitioners for the work, without the priestly ritual that usually accompanied it in Egypt.

wordNotes.term: לַחֲנֹט (lachanot) — to embalm
wordNotes.explanation: The verb chanat in the sense of preserving a body occurs only in this chapter, here and in verse 26 for Joseph himself. The only two people in Scripture said to be embalmed are Jacob and Joseph, father and son, both in Egypt and both destined for burial in Canaan. Israel later buried its dead without such treatment, using spices and linen wrappings, as with Asa and with the body of Jesus.

verses.bibleText: And forty days were fulfilled for him; for so are fulfilled the days of those which are embalmed: and the Egyptians mourned for him threescore and ten days.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two periods are given. Embalming took “forty days,” and the narrator adds that this was the normal time, “for so are fulfilled the days of those which are embalmed.” Then “the Egyptians mourned for him threescore and ten days.” Egyptian records show that the interval between death and burial varied with wealth and period; seventy days appears often as the full span of the funerary process. Whether the forty days are counted inside the seventy or the mourning ran on afterward, the impression is of a long and formal grief observed by the nation.

The subject is striking: “the Egyptians mourned for him.” A people who regarded shepherds as an abomination (46:34) gave a foreign herdsman something close to royal honours. Their regard for Joseph explains much of it; the man who had saved them from starvation (47:25) was honoured through his father. The scene also fulfils, in a small way, the promise that Abraham’s family would bring blessing to the nations (12:3). Jacob had blessed Pharaoh twice (47:7, 10), and Egypt now mourns the man who blessed its king.

Israel would later mourn its own leaders for shorter set periods: thirty days for Aaron (Numbers 20:29) and thirty for Moses (Deuteronomy 34:8). The comparison underlines how lavish this Egyptian mourning was. It also prepares a contrast that the reader of Exodus will feel. A later Pharaoh, who “knew not Joseph” (Exodus 1:8), would turn the honoured guests into slaves. The respect of the world is real but fragile; Israel’s security never rested on it.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּבְכּוּ אֹתוֹ מִצְרַיִם (vayyivku ’oto mitsrayim) — and the Egyptians mourned for him
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “Egypt wept him.” The verb is bakah, the same used of Joseph’s weeping in verse 1, now applied to a whole nation. Israel “wept for Moses” in the plains of Moab for thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8) and the house of Israel mourned Aaron likewise (Numbers 20:29). Here a foreign nation weeps for a patriarch of Israel for seventy.

verses.bibleText: And when the days of his mourning were past, Joseph spake unto the house of Pharaoh, saying, If now I have found grace in your eyes, speak, I pray you, in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
When the mourning was over, Joseph did not go straight to Pharaoh. He “spake unto the house of Pharaoh,” the royal household, and asked them to speak “in the ears of Pharaoh” for him. The reason is not stated. One likely explanation is that a man in mourning, unshaven and in mourning clothes, could not enter the king’s presence; Joseph had once been shaved and changed before he was brought in to Pharaoh (41:14), and later Mordecai could not enter the king’s gate in sackcloth (Esther 4:2). Approaching a ruler through courtiers was also common practice in the East, and it allowed the request to be prepared before it was heard.

There is no hint that Joseph had lost favour. The nation had just mourned his father for seventy days, and Pharaoh’s answer in verse 6 is immediate. Joseph’s courtesy reflects the wisdom that marked his whole career. He speaks the language of petition: “If now I have found grace in your eyes.” The man who governed Egypt still asks rather than demands.

The same phrase had been on Jacob’s lips when he asked Joseph for the oath (47:29). Son now uses with Egypt’s court the words his father used with him. The request that follows is driven by that oath. Joseph’s first loyalty in this matter is to his father’s charge and to the God of the promise behind it, and he uses every proper means to fulfil it.

wordNotes.term: אִם־נָא מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֵיכֶם (’im-na’ matsa’ti chen be‘enekhem) — if now I have found grace in your eyes
wordNotes.explanation: A courteous formula for asking a favour, built on chen, “favour” or “grace.” It is used between people of unequal rank, as when Jacob approached Esau (33:10) and when the dying Jacob asked Joseph to swear (47:29). The same word describes Noah, who “found grace in the eyes of the LORD” (6:8), though there it is God’s unearned favour rather than a polite request.

verses.bibleText: My father made me swear, saying, Lo, I die: in my grave which I have digged for me in the land of Canaan, there shalt thou bury me. Now therefore let me go up, I pray thee, and bury my father, and I will come again.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s message to Pharaoh repeats his father’s charge, but he shapes it for an Egyptian ear. Jacob had said, “bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt” (47:29). Joseph leaves out that refusal, which could have sounded like a slight on the land that had sheltered them, and presents the matter positively: his father had prepared his own grave in Canaan and made his son swear to bury him there. An Egyptian would understand a man’s concern for the tomb he had readied for himself.

“In my grave which I have digged for me” has raised a question, since Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah long before (23:16-20). Jacob may have cut a burial niche for himself within the family cave, or enlarged it. The verb can also mean “acquire,” so the phrase might be rendered “which I have bought for myself,” referring to Jacob’s share in the family tomb. Either way, Jacob had already buried Leah there (49:31), and the place was his by inheritance.

Joseph adds two things. He stresses the oath: “My father made me swear.” An oath sworn to a dying father was sacred, and Pharaoh would respect it. Then he gives his own pledge: “I will come again.” The governor would not use the funeral as a pretext to leave. For Jacob the grave in Canaan was a confession that Egypt was not home; he wished to lie with Abraham and Isaac in the land God had sworn to give (28:13). Joseph faithfully carries that confession to the most powerful man in the world, while keeping his word to serve Pharaoh until God’s appointed time.

wordNotes.term: כָּרִיתִי (kariti) — I have digged
wordNotes.explanation: Karah usually means “to dig,” as of wells (26:25) or a pit. A second verb with the same letters means “to buy” or “to trade,” as in Hosea’s “So I bought her” (Hosea 3:2) and Israel’s buying of water from Edom (Deuteronomy 2:6). Either sense fits: Jacob had prepared, or acquired, a resting place within the cave Abraham purchased.

wordNotes.term: הִשְׁבִּיעַנִי (hishbi‘ani) — made me swear
wordNotes.explanation: The causative of shava‘, “to swear,” meaning to put someone under oath. Abraham made his servant swear about Isaac’s bride (24:3), Jacob made Joseph swear about his burial (47:31), and Joseph will later make the sons of Israel swear about his bones (50:25). In each case the oath binds the next generation to act in line with God’s promise of the land.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said, Go up, and bury thy father, according as he made thee swear.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh’s reply is brief and generous: “Go up, and bury thy father, according as he made thee swear.” He does not haggle or attach conditions, and he does not repeat Joseph’s promise to return, as though it needed no guarantee. The king honours the dead man’s oath and trusts the living man’s word.

The verb “go up” deserves notice. Travel from Egypt to Canaan is consistently “going up” in Scripture, for Canaan lay higher and to the north (13:1; 45:9). Yet the word gathers weight as the story moves on. God had promised Jacob at Beersheba, “I will go down with thee into Egypt; and I will also surely bring thee up again” (46:4). The first fulfilment of that promise is this funeral journey, as Jacob’s body is brought up to the land. A later Pharaoh would refuse to let Israel go up, and God would say to Moses, “I am come down to deliver them … and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land” (Exodus 3:8).

At this point in the story, an Egyptian king freely permits what a later king would resist with all his power. The difference lay in the heart of the ruler, while the God who guided both events was the same.

wordNotes.term: עֲלֵה (‘aleh) — go up
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of ‘alah, “to ascend.” It is the standard verb for leaving Egypt for Canaan (13:1) and becomes a key term of the exodus, when God promises to bring Israel up out of Egypt (Exodus 3:8, 17). Its double use in this chapter (vv. 5-6) and again in Joseph’s final words (v. 24) links Jacob’s funeral with the nation’s later departure.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph went up to bury his father: and with him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph went up to bury his father.” The procession that follows is described at length, beginning with the Egyptians: “all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt.” The repeated “all” conveys a state occasion. Court officials and senior men of the provinces left their duties to accompany the body of a foreign shepherd to a foreign grave. Egyptians were known for elaborate funeral processions, and this one honoured both Pharaoh’s chief minister and his father.

The narrator mentions the Egyptians before the family, and that order says something. Joseph moves between two worlds. He is Pharaoh’s chief minister, and the whole administration follows him; he is also Jacob’s son, and the next verse will name his household and his brothers. The procession displays both identities together on the road to Canaan.

The scene has a forward-looking quality. Israel would one day leave Egypt with “a mixed multitude” going up with them (Exodus 12:38), and God had promised that in Abraham’s seed all the families of the earth would be blessed (22:18). Here the nobility of Egypt walks behind the bier of Israel toward the land of promise. Later prophets would see the nations coming up to honour the God of Israel (Isaiah 2:2-3). In Jacob’s funeral, a foretaste of that gathering is given, though the Egyptians themselves do not yet know the God whose promise they are escorting.

wordNotes.term: זִקְנֵי בֵיתוֹ (ziqne veto) — the elders of his house
wordNotes.explanation: Zaqen, “old” or “elder,” here names senior officials of Pharaoh’s court, men of standing and authority rather than simply aged men. Abraham’s chief steward is called “his eldest servant of his house” (24:2). The same title, “elders,” marks the leaders of Israel whom Moses gathers before the exodus (Exodus 3:16), a parallel the later story will make plain.

verses.bibleText: And all the house of Joseph, and his brethren, and his father's house: only their little ones, and their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Behind the Egyptian dignitaries came the family: “all the house of Joseph, and his brethren, and his father’s house.” Every adult of Israel went up to bury the patriarch. Only “their little ones, and their flocks, and their herds” stayed in Goshen. In practical terms, children and livestock could not easily make so long a journey, and those left behind were also a pledge that the family would come back, as Joseph had promised Pharaoh (v. 5).

The detail carries an irony that the book of Exodus makes plain. When Moses asked that Israel be allowed to go and serve the LORD, Pharaoh first offered to let only the men go, then demanded, “only let your flocks and your herds be stayed: let your little ones also go with you” (Exodus 10:10, 24). Moses refused: “Our cattle also shall go with us; there shall not an hoof be left behind” (Exodus 10:26). At Jacob’s funeral the family leaves little ones and flocks behind and returns to Egypt. At the exodus nothing would be left, because the time of sojourning would be over.

wordNotes.term: טַפָּם (tappam) — their little ones
wordNotes.explanation: Taph refers to young children, often together with the women and dependants of a household. The word appears repeatedly in Pharaoh’s bargaining with Moses (Exodus 10:10, 24), where keeping the little ones in Egypt would have guaranteed Israel’s return. Joseph uses the same word in his promise to nourish his brothers’ little ones (50:21).

verses.bibleText: And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen: and it was a very great company.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen: and it was a very great company.” A funeral escort of chariotry gave dignity and protection on a journey through the desert and into a land outside Egypt’s direct rule. The whole procession is summed up as a “very great” camp, a word that can also mean an army. Its size measured Egypt’s gratitude to Joseph, whose wise management had kept the country alive through seven years of famine, and it also made plain to every onlooker that the governor and his family travelled under Pharaoh’s protection.

Outside this verse, the pairing of Egyptian chariots and horsemen appears in the Pentateuch only in the exodus narrative, where they pursue Israel to the sea and are drowned there (Exodus 14:9, 23; 15:19). Here they ride alongside Israel as an honour guard. The reader who knows the sequel feels the contrast keenly: the same military power that escorted Jacob’s body toward Canaan would one day try to stop his descendants from reaching it, and God would fight for his people (Exodus 14:14).

wordNotes.term: הַמַּחֲנֶה כָּבֵד מְאֹד (hammachaneh kaved me’od) — a very great company
wordNotes.explanation: Machaneh means a camp or encampment, and frequently an army. Jacob named Mahanaim after the camp of God’s angels (32:2), and the word describes the Egyptian host at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:20, 24). Kaved, “heavy,” is repeated in this passage for the “sore” lamentation (v. 10) and the “grievous” mourning (v. 11), giving the whole scene a sense of weight.

verses.bibleText: And they came to the threshingfloor of Atad, which is beyond Jordan, and there they mourned with a great and very sore lamentation: and he made a mourning for his father seven days.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The cortège came to “the threshingfloor of Atad, which is beyond Jordan.” A threshing floor was a broad, level, open space where grain was trampled and winnowed, well suited for a great company to halt. Atad may be the owner’s name, or it may describe the place, since the word means a thorn bush.

“Beyond Jordan” is a relative expression; it can mean either side depending on the speaker. The most natural reading here, with the mourning observed by Canaanites in verse 11, is that the procession had not gone the direct coastal road through Philistine country, nor by way of Beersheba. It swung east around the Dead Sea and reached the Jordan near Jericho. Why it did so is not stated; the security of the southern routes may have been a factor. Whatever the reason, the path the funeral took toward Hebron runs very close to the route Israel would travel under Moses and Joshua, approaching the land from the east and crossing over the Jordan.

There “they mourned with a great and very sore lamentation.” Egyptian tomb paintings show mourners tearing their garments, beating their breasts, and throwing dust on their heads. The narrator stresses the intensity with doubled descriptions: great, and very heavy. Then Joseph “made a mourning for his father seven days.” A week of mourning was customary in Israel and the surrounding world; the men of Jabesh fasted seven days for Saul (1 Samuel 31:13), and Job’s friends sat silent with him seven days (Job 2:13).

This second period of mourning, added to the seventy days in Egypt, shows how fully Jacob was honoured at the end. The man who had once fled from Esau with nothing but a staff (32:10) was carried home in a procession fit for a king. God had kept his promise at Bethel to bring him again into the land (28:15), though Jacob came back as his sons carried him.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּסְפְּדוּ־שָׁם מִסְפֵּד גָּדוֹל וְכָבֵד מְאֹד (vayyispedu-sham misped gadol vekhaved me’od) — they mourned with a great and very sore lamentation
wordNotes.explanation: Saphad means to lament aloud, often with beating of the breast, and misped is the lamentation itself. Abraham came “to mourn for Sarah” with the same verb (23:2), and all Israel lamented Samuel (1 Samuel 25:1). The repetition of verb and noun, with two adjectives, makes the grief emphatic.

wordNotes.term: גֹּרֶן הָאָטָד (goren ha’atad) — the threshingfloor of Atad
wordNotes.explanation: Goren is a threshing floor, an open, levelled space; such places served as gathering points (Ruth 3:2; 2 Samuel 24:18). ’Atad is a thorn or bramble, the plant in Jotham’s fable that offered the trees its shade (Judges 9:14-15). The name may come from thorn bushes growing there or from an owner called Atad.

verses.bibleText: And when the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians: wherefore the name of it was called Abel-mizraim, which is beyond Jordan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The local inhabitants watched. “When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians.” For the people of the land, the spectacle of Egyptian lamentation was so remarkable that it gave the place a new name, Abel-mizraim. The name works on two levels. ’Avel is a common element in place names and likely means a meadow or watercourse, so Abel-mizraim could mean “meadow of Egypt.” Spoken aloud, it also sounded like ’evel mitsrayim, “the mourning of Egypt.” The Canaanites remembered the event by a pun.

The narrator notes that the name was still in use in his own day, a common way in Genesis of tying an event to a known landmark (compare 26:33; 32:32; 35:20). It anchors the story in real geography and memory. The phrase “which is beyond Jordan” is repeated, keeping the reader’s eye on the river that Israel would one day cross.

The scene also bears a silent witness. The Canaanites, who held the land God had promised Abraham, saw a great company of Egyptians mourning a man of Hebrew stock and marking his burial in their country. The promise of the land was still unfulfilled; “the iniquity of the Amorites” was “not yet full” (15:16). Yet Jacob’s body was being laid in the land as a pledge that his descendants would return.

wordNotes.term: אָבֵל מִצְרַיִם (’avel mitsrayim) — Abel-mizraim
wordNotes.explanation: The name plays on two words with the same consonants. ’Avel appears in other place names such as Abel-beth-maachah (2 Samuel 20:14) and Abel-keramim, rendered “the plain of the vineyards” (Judges 11:33), and likely means meadow or brook. ’Evel means mourning, the word Esau used for “the days of mourning for my father” (27:41). The Canaanites heard “mourning of Egypt” in the name.

verses.bibleText: And his sons did unto him according as he commanded them:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And his sons did unto him according as he commanded them.” The sentence takes the reader back to 49:29-32, where Jacob charged all twelve sons to bury him in the cave of Machpelah. Joseph has dominated the account so far; now the narrator turns to “his sons” together. The burial was a family duty, and all of them carried it out. Joseph had the rank to arrange the journey, but the charge had been laid on every son alike, and every son shared in fulfilling it.

The verse is short, but it records an act of obedience by men whose history was full of disobedience and deceit toward their father. They had once brought him a bloodied coat and let him believe a lie (37:31-35). Now they honour his dying word exactly. Faithfulness to a parent’s charge echoes the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12), and the language of doing “according as he commanded” recalls Noah’s obedience to God (6:22). Whatever the brothers’ past, they stood together at their father’s grave as men of their word.

wordNotes.term: כֵּן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּם (ken ka’asher tsiwwam) — according as he commanded them
wordNotes.explanation: Tsawah, “to command” or “charge,” is the verb used for Jacob’s burial instructions in 49:29 and 49:33. The formula of doing just as commanded is used for Noah’s building of the ark (6:22) and for Israel’s completing the tabernacle (Exodus 39:42). It marks complete compliance.

verses.bibleText: For his sons carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field for a possession of a buryingplace of Ephron the Hittite, before Mamre.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For his sons carried him into the land of Canaan.” It seems that the Egyptian escort remained at Atad and only the family went on to Hebron. The sons of Israel enter the land alone, carrying their father, a small picture of the twelve tribes who would one day cross the Jordan without Egypt’s company.

The burial place is described with full legal detail: “the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field for a possession of a buryingplace of Ephron the Hittite, before Mamre.” The narrator repeats almost word for word the terms of the purchase in chapter 23. Abraham had insisted on paying the full price before witnesses (23:16-18), refusing a gift, so that his family’s claim would be beyond dispute. That cave was the only part of Canaan the patriarchs ever owned. Abraham and Sarah lay there, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah (49:31). Now Jacob joined them, as he had asked.

The repetition is an assertion of faith. God had promised Abraham, “unto thy seed will I give this land” (12:7), and “an everlasting possession” (17:8). The patriarchs died without seeing that promise fulfilled. Hebrews says they “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Hebrews 11:13). Their graves in Canaan were a down payment, a small plot held in hope of the whole. To be buried there was to declare that the God who made the promise would keep it.

The Christian reads such graves in the light of Christ’s own tomb near Jerusalem, emptied on the third day. Those who sleep in Jesus are laid down in the same hope, and God will bring them again (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

wordNotes.term: אֲחֻזַּת־קָבֶר (’achuzzat-qever) — a possession of a buryingplace
wordNotes.explanation: ’Achuzzah is property held as one’s own, a legal holding. Abraham asked the Hittites for “a possession of a buryingplace” (23:4), and the field “was made sure” to him as such (23:20). The same noun stands in God’s promise of Canaan as “an everlasting possession” (17:8). The burial plot was the first, small portion of that promised holding.

wordNotes.term: מְעָרַת שְׂדֵה הַמַּכְפֵּלָה (me‘arat sedeh hammakhpelah) — the cave of the field of Machpelah
wordNotes.explanation: Makhpelah is always used with the article, perhaps describing the cave as “the double one.” It lay near Mamre, that is, Hebron (23:19). The name occurs only in Genesis, each time in connection with the patriarchal burials (25:9; 49:30), which made it a lasting landmark of the promise.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph returned into Egypt, he, and his brethren, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph returned into Egypt, he, and his brethren, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father.” Joseph keeps his word to Pharaoh (v. 5). The order of names has changed from verses 7-8: there the Egyptian officials came first; here, after the burial, the family is named first and the others follow.

They went back because the time to possess the land had not come. God had told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in a land not theirs and afflicted four hundred years, and that “in the fourth generation they shall come hither again” (15:13-16). He had told Jacob, “fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation” (46:3). The family was not yet a nation. Returning to Egypt after burying Jacob was itself an act of trust that God’s timing was right. Joseph had glimpsed the land again and stood by his father’s grave; then he went back to serve where God had placed him, waiting for the day his own bones would make the same journey.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּשָׁב יוֹסֵף מִצְרַיְמָה (vayyashov yosef mitsraymah) — and Joseph returned into Egypt
wordNotes.explanation: Shuv, “to return,” is the verb of Joseph’s promise, “I will come again” (v. 5). It also appears in God’s word to Abraham that his seed would “come hither again” in the fourth generation (15:16), and in God’s promise to Jacob to bring him “again into this land” (28:15). Joseph returns to Egypt now; Israel will return to Canaan later.

verses.bibleText: And when Joseph's brethren saw that their father was dead, they said, Joseph will peradventure hate us, and will certainly requite us all the evil which we did unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Back in Egypt, with the funeral over, the brothers faced a new fear. “When Joseph’s brethren saw that their father was dead, they said, Joseph will peradventure hate us, and will certainly requite us all the evil which we did unto him.” Seventeen years had passed since Joseph wept on their necks and told them not to be grieved or angry with themselves (45:5, 15). He had settled them in Goshen and fed them and their children throughout the famine. Yet they wondered whether all that kindness had been for Jacob’s sake, and whether Joseph had only postponed his revenge until the old man was gone.

They had a model for such fears in their own family. Esau had said, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then will I slay my brother Jacob” (27:41). The brothers may have supposed that Joseph thought the same way. Their fear says more about their own consciences than about anything Joseph had done. Guilt that has never fully accepted forgiveness keeps expecting punishment. They name their deed honestly, “all the evil which we did unto him,” but they cannot yet rest in the mercy shown them.

The brothers’ anxiety is a common human experience before God as well. Many who have heard the gospel of free forgiveness still live as though God were waiting for an opportunity to repay them. Scripture answers that fear with God’s own word: “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12), and “perfect love casteth out fear” (1 John 4:18). Joseph will need to tell his brothers again what he told them before, and God is patient in the same way with those slow to believe his grace.

wordNotes.term: לוּ יִשְׂטְמֵנוּ יוֹסֵף (lu yistemenu yosef) — Joseph will peradventure hate us
wordNotes.explanation: Satam means to bear a grudge or cherish hostility, the kind of hatred that waits for its opportunity. It describes Esau’s hatred of Jacob after the stolen blessing (27:41), and in Jacob’s blessing it is used of the archers who “hated” Joseph (49:23). The particle lu here expresses a fearful supposition: “what if Joseph bears a grudge against us?”

wordNotes.term: וְהָשֵׁב יָשִׁיב לָנוּ (vehashev yashiv lanu) — and will certainly requite us
wordNotes.explanation: The verb shuv in its causative form means to bring back or repay, and the doubled form adds certainty. It is used for paying back wrong for wrong (Psalm 54:5), a course Scripture forbids to the injured party: “Say not thou, I will recompense evil; but wait on the LORD” (Proverbs 20:22). Joseph will take exactly that path.

verses.bibleText: And they sent a messenger unto Joseph, saying, Thy father did command before he died, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers did not go to Joseph directly. “They sent a messenger unto Joseph.” The Hebrew reads more literally “they charged Joseph” or “they sent a charge to Joseph,” using the same verb that described Jacob’s commands to his sons (49:29, 33). They prepared the way through a go-between, much as Jacob had sent messengers and gifts ahead before meeting Esau (32:3-5).

The message begins with an appeal to their father: “Thy father did command before he died, saying.” Genesis records no such instruction, and some readers have taken it as an invention born of fear. Yet the narrator does not call it false, and Joseph does not question it. It would not be surprising for Jacob, aware of the brothers’ guilt and fear, to have urged them to seek Joseph’s pardon. The silence of Jacob’s final blessings about the sale of Joseph may also suggest that the old man had already forgiven the crime that God had turned into the family’s deliverance. The point the text makes clear is that the brothers took shelter behind their father’s authority, the authority Joseph had just honoured by burying him in Canaan.

They also say “thy father,” not “our father.” The phrase reminds Joseph of the bond he shared with Jacob, the father who loved him most, and appeals to that love on their behalf. Even in fear they found the most persuasive words available.

wordNotes.term: וַיְצַוּוּ אֶל־יוֹסֵף (vaytsawwu ’el-yosef) — and they sent a messenger unto Joseph
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “they commanded to Joseph,” meaning they sent instructions or a message by others. The verb tsawah appears twice in this verse, first for the brothers’ message and then for Jacob’s alleged command, echoing its use for Jacob’s real charge about his burial (49:29, 33). The brothers borrow the language of a father’s solemn charge.

verses.bibleText: So shall ye say unto Joseph, Forgive, I pray thee now, the trespass of thy brethren, and their sin; for they did unto thee evil: and now, we pray thee, forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father. And Joseph wept when they spake unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The message continues with the words the brothers attribute to Jacob: “So shall ye say unto Joseph, Forgive, I pray thee now, the trespass of thy brethren, and their sin; for they did unto thee evil.” For the first time in the whole story the brothers ask Joseph to forgive them. In chapter 42 they confessed among themselves, “We are verily guilty concerning our brother” (42:21); in chapter 44 Judah confessed before the unrecognized governor that “God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants” (44:16). At the reconciliation in chapter 45 Joseph spoke words of comfort, but the brothers said nothing. Now they name their deed with the strongest terms Hebrew has: “trespass,” a wilful breach of relationship, and “sin.” They add plainly, “they did unto thee evil.”

Then comes their own plea: “and now, we pray thee, forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father.” They appeal to a shared faith. Whatever they had done, they were worshippers of the same God as Joseph and Jacob. In Scripture forgiveness of sin is above all God’s act (Exodus 34:7); the God who forgives makes it possible for his servants to forgive one another (Ephesians 4:32).

“And Joseph wept when they spake unto him.” This is the last of Joseph’s many weepings in Genesis. The text does not explain the tears, but the context suggests grief that his brothers still doubted him. After years of kindness they feared he had been nursing a grudge. Forgiveness offered and not believed wounds the one who gave it.

Jesus told the parable of a servant forgiven an enormous debt and warned that the forgiven must forgive (Matthew 18:21-35). The brothers come to Joseph as debtors; Joseph has long since cancelled the debt. Their request, though late, is right, for confession opens the way to rest in a pardon already granted.

wordNotes.term: שָׂא נָא לְפֶשַׁע (sa’ na’ lefesha‘) — forgive, I pray thee, the trespass
wordNotes.explanation: Nasa’, “to lift” or “carry,” is a common way of saying “forgive” when its object is sin: the guilt is lifted off and borne away. God describes himself as “forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin” with this verb (Exodus 34:7), and David blesses the one “whose transgression is forgiven” (Psalm 32:1). Pesha‘, here rendered “trespass,” denotes rebellion or breach of a relationship (31:36).

wordNotes.term: עַבְדֵי אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ (‘avde ’elohe ’avikha) — the servants of the God of thy father
wordNotes.explanation: The brothers identify themselves by their relationship to the family’s God. The title “God of thy father” is the one God used when he spoke to Jacob at Beersheba (46:3), and Jacob blessed Joseph by “the God of thy father” (49:25). The word ‘eved, “servant,” recurs in the next verse when the brothers call themselves Joseph’s servants.

verses.bibleText: And his brethren also went and fell down before his face; and they said, Behold, we be thy servants.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the message came the brothers themselves. “And his brethren also went and fell down before his face; and they said, Behold, we be thy servants.” Perhaps Joseph’s tears, reported back to them, gave them courage to come in person. They bowed to the ground and offered themselves as slaves.

The scene completes a pattern that began with a teenage dream. Joseph saw his brothers’ sheaves bow down to his sheaf (37:7), and they answered with scorn: “Shalt thou indeed reign over us?” They bowed to him in Egypt without knowing him (42:6; 43:26), and after Benjamin was caught with the cup they fell before him and offered to be his bondmen (44:14, 16). Now they bow once more, knowing exactly who he is, and say, “we be thy servants.” The men who sold their brother as a slave are ready to become his slaves.

Joseph never asked for this. His dreams had come true, but he had no wish to rule his brothers by fear. The New Testament speaks of a greater Son who also came to his own and was rejected, who was “sold” for silver and handed to foreigners, and who now receives the homage of those who once despised him (Philippians 2:9-11). Yet he too calls those who come to him no longer servants but friends (John 15:15). Exaltation in God’s kingdom is used for service and rescue, never for revenge.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְּלוּ לְפָנָיו (vayyippelu lefanayw) — and fell down before his face
wordNotes.explanation: Naphal, “to fall,” with “before his face” describes full prostration. The same verb was used when the brothers “fell before him on the ground” after the cup was found (44:14). It echoes the bowing of the sheaves in Joseph’s first dream (37:7), now carried out in full knowledge and humility.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s reply begins with comfort: “Fear not.” It is the reassurance God himself gave to Abraham (15:1), to Isaac (26:24), and to Jacob as he set out for Egypt (46:3). On Joseph’s lips it carries the same meaning: there is nothing to be afraid of.

Then comes a question: “for am I in the place of God?” The form expects the answer no. Jacob had used the same words in anger when Rachel demanded children: “Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” (30:2). Joseph uses them to set himself on the same level as his brothers. Their message had treated him almost as God’s representative, asking him to “forgive” and calling themselves his servants. Joseph refuses the role.

The question works in two directions. First, judgment and vengeance belong to God alone. “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence,” says the LORD (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Paul quotes the verse to tell believers not to avenge themselves (Romans 12:19). Joseph will not take into his hands a right that is God’s. Second, God had already passed judgment on the matter by turning it to good, as the next verse explains. For Joseph to punish what God had overruled for salvation would be to set himself above God’s verdict.

This is the root of Joseph’s forgiveness. He did not deny the wrong or pretend it did not hurt. He gave up the right to settle the account himself, because he trusted the One who sits on the throne. Peter writes that Christ, when he suffered, “threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). Joseph walked in that path long before it was trodden perfectly at the cross.

wordNotes.term: הֲתַחַת אֱלֹהִים אָנִי (hatachat ’elohim ’ani) — am I in the place of God?
wordNotes.explanation: Tachath means “under” and then “in place of.” The question appears in identical form in Jacob’s retort to Rachel (30:2). A similar protest is made by the king of Israel when asked to cure Naaman: “Am I God, to kill and to make alive?” (2 Kings 5:7). Each time a human being disclaims a power that belongs to God alone.

wordNotes.term: אַל־תִּירָאוּ (’al-tira’u) — fear not
wordNotes.explanation: The negative command of yare’, “to fear,” is one of the most frequent assurances in Scripture, usually spoken by God. God said it to Abraham (15:1), Isaac (26:24), and Jacob (46:3). Joseph repeats it twice in this exchange (vv. 19, 21), framing his explanation of God’s purpose.

verses.bibleText: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here is the theological heart of the Joseph story and one of the great sentences of Genesis: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” Joseph sets two intentions side by side. The brothers planned evil; God planned good. The same verb serves both: they “thought” evil, God “meant” it, literally “thought it,” for good. Both plans concerned the same events: the pit, the sale, the slavery, the prison.

Joseph does not soften the guilt. “Ye thought evil” uses the word the brothers themselves used in verse 17. Their hatred was real, their choice was free, and their deed was evil. God did not make them sin, nor does the good outcome excuse what they did; that is why they needed forgiveness. What Joseph declares is that God was not defeated by their sin. He took the evil they intended and wove it into his purpose, so that the very act meant to destroy Joseph put him where he could save them. Joseph had said the same when he made himself known: “God did send me before you to preserve life” (45:5-8).

The purpose is stated: “to save much people alive.” Egypt, the neighbouring peoples who came for grain, and the family from which the Messiah would come were all kept alive. God’s good is concrete; it is measured in lives preserved.

This verse is a window into how Scripture speaks of providence everywhere. “Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee” (Psalm 76:10). Paul writes that “all things work together for good to them that love God” (Romans 8:28), not because all things are good, but because God works in them toward his purpose. Above all, the pattern finds its fullest expression at the cross. Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem that Jesus was “delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,” and in the same breath, “ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain” (Acts 2:23). The betrayal, the false trial, the crucifixion were the work of wicked hands, and God made them the salvation of the world. Christ, like Joseph, was rejected by his brothers and handed to Gentiles, and through his suffering many are saved alive.

For the believer this verse gives no license to call evil good, or to rush a suffering person toward a tidy explanation. Joseph spoke these words after more than twenty years, looking back. It gives a reason to trust, in the middle of the story, that the God who governed Joseph’s pit and prison also governs ours, and that the last word belongs to him.

wordNotes.term: חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה (chashavtem ‘alay ra‘ah ’elohim chashavah letovah) — ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good
wordNotes.explanation: Chashav means to think, plan, or devise. Used with ra‘ah, “evil,” it describes plotting harm (Micah 2:1); used of God it describes his settled purposes, as in “the thoughts that I think toward you … thoughts of peace, and not of evil” (Jeremiah 29:11). The repetition of one verb for two subjects sets human scheming and divine purpose over the same events, with God’s purpose prevailing (Psalm 33:10-11).

wordNotes.term: לְהַחֲיֹת עַם־רָב (lehachayot ‘am-rav) — to save much people alive
wordNotes.explanation: The causative of chayah, “to live,” means to keep alive or preserve life. Joseph used related words at the reconciliation: “God did send me before you to preserve life” and “to save your lives by a great deliverance” (45:5, 7). The Egyptians thanked him, “Thou hast saved our lives” (47:25), using the same verb.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph draws the practical conclusion: “Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones.” Because God had overruled the evil for good, there was no reason for fear and no ground for vengeance. The “I” is emphatic. Joseph himself will continue to provide for them and their children, as he had done since they came to Egypt (45:11; 47:12).

He does more than refrain from harm. He repays evil with good. His brothers had once taken from him his coat, his freedom, and his home; he now promises them bread and protection for their families. The famine was long past, but the brothers lived as foreigners in Egypt, and their security still depended on their powerful brother. Joseph pledges that it would not fail. Jesus taught the same way: “do good to them that hate you” (Luke 6:27), and Paul, “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

“And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.” Literally, he “spoke to their heart.” The expression is used for words that reach the inner person and reassure them, as when Boaz spoke kindly to Ruth (Ruth 2:13), or when God says, “Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:2). Joseph’s forgiveness was complete enough to address their fear, not only their offence.

This is the final glimpse of Joseph with his brothers. The story that began with brothers who “could not speak peaceably unto him” (37:4) ends with Joseph speaking to his brothers’ hearts. Hatred has been answered with tenderness, and the family of Israel stands reconciled.

wordNotes.term: וַיְדַבֵּר עַל־לִבָּם (vaydabber ‘al-libbam) — and spake kindly unto them
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “spoke upon their heart.” The idiom describes words meant to win, reassure, or comfort someone, often after hurt or estrangement. Shechem spoke to Dinah’s heart (34:3), Boaz spoke to Ruth’s heart (Ruth 2:13), and God tells the prophet to speak to Jerusalem’s heart after her punishment (Isaiah 40:2).

wordNotes.term: אֲכַלְכֵּל (’akhalkel) — I will nourish
wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of kul, meaning to sustain or provide for, especially with food. Joseph used the same verb when he first invited his family to Egypt (45:11), and the narrator says that Joseph “nourished” his father and household with bread (47:12). David’s promise to Barzillai uses the same verb (2 Samuel 19:32).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he, and his father's house: and Joseph lived an hundred and ten years.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he, and his father’s house: and Joseph lived an hundred and ten years.” The narrative moves swiftly over the decades. Joseph was about fifty-six when Jacob died (he was thirty at his promotion, thirty-nine when Jacob arrived, and Jacob lived seventeen years in Egypt), so he lived another fifty-four years. The family that had come for a famine stayed on, and Joseph remained in Egypt with them.

The span of 110 years matched what Egyptian texts held to be the ideal length of a blessed life, and a reader in Egypt would hear it as a mark of a life fully honoured. Joshua, who led Israel into the land Joseph never saw again, died at the same age (Joshua 24:29). Joseph’s years were fewer than those of Abraham (175), Isaac (180), or Jacob (147), but they were full. The boy sold at seventeen lived to see the long fulfilment of God’s purposes in his life, as the psalm says of those who trust the Lord: “With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation” (Psalm 91:16).

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּשֶׁב יוֹסֵף בְּמִצְרַיִם (vayyeshev yosef bemitsrayim) — and Joseph dwelt in Egypt
wordNotes.explanation: Yashav, “to sit” or “dwell,” describes settled residence. The Joseph story opened with “Jacob dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger, in the land of Canaan” (37:1), and Israel later “dwelt in the land of Egypt” (47:27). The story that began with dwelling in Canaan ends with dwelling in Egypt, awaiting the return.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation: the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation.” Whether this means Ephraim’s great-grandchildren or his grandchildren depends on how the generations are counted; the phrase “third and fourth generation” in the commandments includes the father’s line in different ways (Exodus 20:5; 34:7). Either way, Joseph lived to see his family multiply over several generations, a sign of God’s blessing. “Children’s children are the crown of old men” (Proverbs 17:6), and the psalmist prays, “thou shalt see thy children’s children” (Psalm 128:6). Jacob’s blessing on Joseph as “a fruitful bough” (49:22) was already coming true.

“The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph’s knees.” Literally they were “born upon Joseph’s knees.” The phrase recalls Rachel’s words about Bilhah, “she shall bear upon my knees” (30:3), and Jacob’s taking Ephraim and Manasseh between his knees (48:12). It may describe Joseph receiving the newborns as his own, a gesture of acknowledgment or adoption. Machir’s line became one of the most important clans of Manasseh, and in Deborah’s song Machir stands for the whole tribe (Judges 5:14).

wordNotes.term: בְּנֵי שִׁלֵּשִׁים (bene shilleshim) — children of the third generation
wordNotes.explanation: Shilleshim denotes members of the third generation. The same word appears in the second commandment, where God visits iniquity “unto the third and fourth generation” of those who hate him (Exodus 20:5), and in God’s self-revelation to Moses (Exodus 34:7; Numbers 14:18). Here it marks blessing rather than judgment.

wordNotes.term: יֻלְּדוּ עַל־בִּרְכֵּי יוֹסֵף (yulledu ‘al-birke yosef) — brought up upon Joseph’s knees
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “were born upon Joseph’s knees.” Placing a newborn on one’s knees could signal acceptance into the family line. Rachel used the idea for Bilhah’s children (30:3), and Jacob drew Joseph’s sons from between his knees when he adopted them (48:12). Job’s lament, “Why did the knees prevent me?” pictures the newborn received on the knees (Job 3:12).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s last recorded words follow the pattern of his father’s. “And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” Jacob had said almost the same to Joseph: “Behold, I die: but God shall be with you, and bring you again unto the land of your fathers” (48:21). The faith of one generation is handed to the next at the deathbed.

“His brethren” may include surviving brothers, or more broadly his kinsmen, the next generation of Israel. Joseph speaks plainly about his death. He does not cling to life or fear its end, but turns at once from his own death to God’s future: “God will surely visit you.” Joseph knew that Israel’s ease in Egypt depended on his presence, and he may have sensed hard days coming. God had told Abraham that his seed would be afflicted in a strange land and that afterward “shall they come out with great substance” (15:13-14). Joseph’s words rest on that prophecy.

For the first time in Scripture the three patriarchs are named together: “Abraham, … Isaac, and … Jacob.” The phrase will become the standard way of referring to the covenant God. At the burning bush he identifies himself as “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6), and Jesus uses the same title to prove the resurrection of the dead, since God “is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). The patriarchs lay in the grave, but God’s covenant with them guaranteed that they would live again.

Genesis thus ends on expectation. The promise of the land is unfulfilled, the family is in Egypt, and its leader is dying, yet his last word is a confident “God will surely visit you.” Generations later Zacharias would praise the Lord God of Israel, “for he hath visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68), as the Redeemer came. The church still waits for the final visitation, when Christ returns.

wordNotes.term: פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד (paqod yifqod) — will surely visit
wordNotes.explanation: Paqad means to attend to, take note of, or intervene in someone’s situation, for blessing or for judgment. “The LORD visited Sarah” when he gave her Isaac (21:1). God commands Moses to tell Israel, “I have surely visited you” with the same doubled form (Exodus 3:16), and the people believed “that the LORD had visited the children of Israel” (Exodus 4:31). The Greek Old Testament uses the verb Luke chooses for Christ’s coming (Luke 1:68).

wordNotes.term: אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּע לְאַבְרָהָם לְיִצְחָק וּלְיַעֲקֹב (’asher nishba‘ le’avraham leyitschaq uleya‘aqov) — which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob
wordNotes.explanation: Nishba‘, “he swore,” describes God binding himself by oath. God swore to Abraham after the offering of Isaac (22:16) and confirmed the oath to Isaac (26:3). In Exodus he promises to bring Israel into the land “concerning the which I did swear to give it to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob” (Exodus 6:8).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.” Jacob had asked to be carried to Canaan at once; Joseph asked something different. He did not request immediate burial in the land, as his father had. Perhaps his position in Egypt made that impossible, or perhaps he knew the family must stay. Instead he bound the people to take his remains with them when God brought them out. His body would wait in Egypt and go up with the nation.

The request is an act of faith. Hebrews singles it out: “By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel; and gave commandment concerning his bones” (Hebrews 11:22). Out of all Joseph’s life, the dreams, the purity, the wisdom, the forgiveness, the writer chose this deathbed word, because it showed that Joseph believed God’s promise more than Egypt’s honours. He was the most powerful man in Egypt and could have had a magnificent tomb there. He chose to have his bones wait for the exodus.

The oath was kept. When Israel left Egypt generations later, “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel” (Exodus 13:19), repeating Joseph’s very words. The bones went through the sea and the wilderness, and after the conquest they were buried at Shechem, in the plot Jacob had bought and given to Joseph (Joshua 24:32; Genesis 33:19).

Joseph’s concern for his bones also expresses hope beyond the exodus. He did not expect to live on in some other world while his body lay in Egypt; Scripture describes the dead as sleeping in the dust until God awakens them (Daniel 12:2). His bones would rest in the land of promise awaiting that day. The faithful dead, Hebrews says, “received not the promise” in their lifetime, so that “they without us should not be made perfect” (Hebrews 11:39-40). They will rise together with all God’s people when Christ comes (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

wordNotes.term: עַצְמֹתַי (‘atsmotay) — my bones
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Etsem, “bone,” is often used for the remains of the dead. The word ties Joseph’s request to its fulfilment in Exodus, where Moses takes Joseph’s bones (Exodus 13:19), and in Joshua, where they are buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). In Elisha’s tomb a dead man revived on touching the prophet’s bones (2 Kings 13:21), and Ezekiel saw dry bones live again by God’s word (Ezekiel 37:5).

wordNotes.term: וַיַּשְׁבַּע יוֹסֵף (vayyashba‘ yosef) — and Joseph took an oath
wordNotes.explanation: The causative of shava‘ means to make someone swear. Jacob made Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (47:31), and now Joseph makes the next generation swear. Exodus says Moses carried the bones because Joseph “had straitly sworn the children of Israel,” using the doubled form of the same verb (Exodus 13:19).

verses.bibleText: So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.” The final verse of Genesis is brief and restrained. Joseph’s death is reported in a single clause, his age repeated from verse 22. Like his father, he was embalmed, prepared by Egyptian skill for a journey Egypt knew nothing about.

The last words, “in a coffin in Egypt,” hold the whole tension of the book’s ending. The coffin was probably a wooden case, perhaps shaped to the body in Egyptian fashion, and it was not buried in Canaan as Jacob’s body had been. It remained among the Israelites in Egypt, a standing reminder through the years of hardship that followed. Every generation that saw it or heard of it was reminded that Joseph had expected God to visit them, and that they were to carry him out when he did. While the coffin stayed in Egypt, the story was unfinished.

The ending looks straight forward to the exodus. Exodus opens by recalling that “Joseph died, and all his brethren” (Exodus 1:6), and then describes a new king who did not know Joseph. Oppression follows, then God’s visitation, the plagues, the Passover, and the night when Moses took Joseph’s bones (Exodus 13:19). Genesis is a book of beginnings, and its last line is itself a beginning: the people of promise wait in a foreign land with a coffin and a promise.

The contrast with the book’s opening is striking. Genesis began with God creating life, breathing into man the breath of life in a garden. It ends with a man in a coffin, because sin brought death into the world (Romans 5:12). Yet death is not given the final word. Joseph dies trusting a God who visits, and Scripture speaks of the righteous dead as asleep, resting without consciousness until the resurrection (Daniel 12:2; John 11:11). Joseph’s coffin, like Jacob’s grave, waits for God to keep his word.

That word has its fullest answer in Christ. He too was laid in a tomb, but it held him only three days; he rose as “the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Corinthians 15:20). When he comes again, the dead in Christ will rise, and every coffin of the faithful will be emptied. The final exodus will lead God’s people out of death itself into the land he has promised.

wordNotes.term: בָּאָרוֹן (ba’aron) — in a coffin
wordNotes.explanation: ’Aron is a chest or box. It is the word for the chest Jehoiada placed at the temple gate to receive offerings (2 Kings 12:9) and, most often, for the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:10; Deuteronomy 10:5). Only here is it used for a coffin. During the wilderness journey Israel carried both the ark containing God’s law and the chest containing Joseph’s bones.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּחַנְטוּ אֹתוֹ (vayyachantu ’oto) — and they embalmed him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb chanat, used for Jacob in verse 2, appears here for the last time in Scripture. Joseph is the only other person in the Bible said to be embalmed. His preservation served the same purpose as his father’s: to allow his body to wait in Egypt and be carried to Canaan when God fulfilled his word (Exodus 13:19).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can a person look back on the worst wrong done to them and say that God meant it for good?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God keeps his promises through death and overrules human sin for good; Joseph therefore forgives without taking God’s place, and dies looking forward to the day God will visit his people and bring them home.
discussionQuestions: Why did Jacob and Joseph both insist on burial in Canaan rather than in the honoured tombs of Egypt?
Why were the brothers still afraid of Joseph seventeen years after he had forgiven them, and what does that reveal about receiving forgiveness?
What does Joseph mean by asking, “Am I in the place of God?” and how does that question free him to forgive?
How does 50:20 hold together the brothers’ real guilt and God’s sovereign purpose, and how does the cross show the same pattern?
What did Joseph’s coffin say to Israel during the long years in Egypt, and what does the believer’s grave say today?
commonMisunderstandings: Saying that God meant evil for good does not make the evil less evil; Joseph calls the brothers’ deed evil and God turns it, which is different from approving it.
Embalming Jacob did not mean Joseph adopted Egyptian beliefs about the afterlife; the body was prepared for a journey to the land of promise.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending nothing happened; Joseph names the wrong and still refuses revenge.
Joseph’s charge about his bones does not suggest he expected to live on elsewhere meanwhile; he rests in death until God’s visitation, the hope later made plain in the resurrection.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep 50:20 at the centre, but set it within the chapter’s frame of two deaths and two burials. The same God who turned the brothers’ crime into the saving of many lives will keep his word to bring Israel up from Egypt and, in the end, to raise his sleeping people.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Lay down the wrongs you have been holding, leave judgment with God who alone sits in his own place, and live and die as Joseph did, trusting that God will surely visit his people.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s sovereign providence and his faithfulness beyond death: he overrules sin for salvation, supremely at the cross, and he will keep his promise to raise those who sleep in hope.
flow: Joseph’s brothers sold him out of hatred, and the evil was real and deliberate.
God turned that evil into the means of saving many lives, so that Joseph could say, “God meant it unto good.”
At the cross human wickedness did its worst, and God made it the salvation of the world.
Because judgment belongs to God, the forgiven can forgive, and the fearful can rest in grace freely given.
Joseph died trusting God’s promise and asked that his bones be carried home; the believer sleeps in the same hope until Christ comes and raises the dead.
simpleIllustrations: A weaver works from the back of the tapestry, where knots and loose ends are all one sees; turned over, the same threads show the design.
A family kept a packed trunk by the door for years because they had been promised passage home; Joseph’s coffin was Israel’s packed trunk.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the God who turns evil to good, receive his forgiveness for your own wrongs, and wait in hope for the day he raises his people?
cautions: Do not tell a person who is suffering that their pain is good; Scripture names wrong for what it is and says God works through it.
Avoid suggesting that the brothers’ sin was excused by its good outcome; they still needed and sought forgiveness.
Present the hope of the dead as resurrection at Christ’s coming, not as immediate passage to heaven.

reflectionQuestions: Is there a wrong done to me that I still want to repay, and am I trying to sit in God’s place?
Do I believe God’s forgiveness, or do I keep waiting for the punishment I think is still coming?
Where can I look back and see God bringing good out of something meant for harm?
Does the way I face death, and plan for it, show that I trust God’s promises?
What am I passing on to the next generation about the God who will surely visit his people?
